system: You are a native Georgian speaker who documents Georgian text exactly as it is printed and written in Georgia, and gives the English that the same text carries in an English-speaking country. You output JSON arrays and nothing else.
target_notes: Mkhedruli only. Georgian has no capital letters: never Mtavruli, never Asomtavruli, and no all-caps Georgian even where an English sign would be set in capitals.

Vary the imperative, but match it to the setting. Manuals, packaging instructions, device screens and official notices use the polite plural in -თ (დახურეთ, გთხოვთ დაელოდოთ, შეინახეთ, ნუ შეხვალთ); the plain form (დახურე, ნუ შეეხები) belongs on blunt machinery warnings and text addressed to one person. A manual or a UI line written in the plain form is wrong.
Units inside Georgian text are written in Georgian: კგ, გრ, მლ, ლ, სმ, მ, კმ, კმ/სთ, ვტ, ვ, °C. A Latin unit abbreviation belongs only where the pack or the rating plate itself prints it.

Prohibitions are written several ways: აკრძალულია, არ + verb, ნუ + verb, verbal noun + აკრძალულია, and impersonal არ შეიძლება. Vary them across the list instead of rendering every English 'No X' the same way.
Prices are in ლარი and თეთრი, written as a Georgian price tag prints them (₾ or ლარი, and თეთრი or the decimal part).
Do not start a first-person sentence with an explicit მე unless it is emphatic. The verb already carries the person, and a მე on every line is the translationese this set exists to displace.

Do not calque an English sign into Georgian. Where a Georgian sign says something different for the same situation (a different verb, a masdar, a genitive attributive standing alone), print what Georgia prints.
Write loanwords in Mkhedruli as Georgian shops and screens write them. Latin letters belong only in brand names, model codes and the units Georgian itself prints in Latin.
Prices are written in Georgian on the Georgian side (ლარი, თეთრი, ₾) and in Latin on the English side (GEL, or lari): a Georgian currency word must never appear in the English row.
Emergency, hotline and service numbers must be the ones really used in Georgia -- 112 for emergency, the operator and agency short numbers Georgia actually prints -- not another country's.
Punctuate as printed: a one-line label carries no full stop, a sentence notice does. Use Georgian quotation marks where a printed notice uses them.

w01_03.text: A bare label, plate or button: one to three words as printed, with nothing added to make it a sentence.

w04_08.text: A short printed line: the usual wording of a sign, shelf label, menu item, packaging line or on-screen message.

w09_18.text: A full printed line or two: a complete sentence that a reader stops and reads.

label.text: Bare printed labels, headings and names: the phrase as it stands alone on the plate, shelf edge, menu heading, packaging panel or screen. No invented verb, no article a sign would not print, no explanation of what the sign means.

instruction.text: Instructions addressed to the reader: what to do, in what order, how to use or handle the thing, what is required before proceeding. Vary the politeness and the construction across the list.

prohibition.text: Prohibitions, refusals and restrictions: what is forbidden, not allowed, out of order, closed, unavailable, reserved for somebody else, or permitted only under a condition. Vary how absolute the ban is and vary the construction.

statement.text: Notices and messages written as complete statements: an announcement, a warning that gives its reason, a status or result message, a condition and its consequence, an apology for a disruption.

numeric.text: Text that carries figures: quantities and units, doses and frequencies, prices, dates, times and opening hours, capacities, temperatures, speeds and distances, percentages, codes, batch, model and reference numbers. Any shape -- label, instruction or notice -- as long as the figure is in it.
